stories.title: Mercy
stories.body:
March 20, 2020
20:40

Garage
-- S1 --

JAKOVIC taps the kick drum, listens, then tightens the pedal. Still not right. He leans forward, gives it another tap, then adjusts the setting again.

Meanwhile, DOUGLAS sits beside AMELIE at the piano, going through a few notes together. CHERLINE pulls the microphone closer to her mouth, then shifts around on the stool she is sitting on.

ANDREA : Row. Row. Row.
ANDREA warms up his voice, testing a few notes under his breath. He plucks the string down one note.

ANDREA : Row. Fucking hell.
He stops, stares at the guitar for a second, then puts it down beside him.

ANDREA : G minor's fine. It's just... something feels off with the arrangement.
CHERLINE : What part?
CHERLINE tilts her head, waiting.

ANDREA : The guitar, mostly. When everything comes in, I can't really sit with the vocal.
CHERLINE : Too loud?
ANDREA : Kinda. Not really.
He rubs his jaw, trying to find the right words.

ANDREA : It's just there all the time. I push the vocal, it gets in the way. I pull back, and the whole thing loses something.
DOUGLAS : So what, you want me to play less?
DOUGLAS glances over his shoulder at him, one eyebrow slightly raised.

ANDREA : A little, yeah. Just give me some room.
DOUGLAS : Alright.
DOUGLAS lowers his hand towards the strings.

ANDREA : Not that much.
DOUGLAS stops and looks at him.

DOUGLAS : Jesus. Make up your mind.
ANDREA : I'm trying to.
ANDREA gives him a tired look. DOUGLAS shakes his head with a small grin and plays the progression again, this time softer.

ANDREA starts singing.

He gets through the verse without stopping.

ANDREA : Yeah. That's better.
He looks towards DOUGLAS and gives a small nod.

CHERLINE : Yeah, actually.
ANDREA : The verse, anyway.
CHERLINE : What's wrong with the chorus?
ANDREA : It just jumps out too much. When everything comes in, it gets way too bright.
DOUGLAS looks down at his guitar and plays the last part of the progression again, listening to it.

DOUGLAS : Yeah... I kinda hear it.
ANDREA : See.
DOUGLAS : Don't get too excited.
ANDREA : Shut up.
AMELIE shifts closer to the piano, resting one hand on the edge of it.

AMELIE : We could change the chords when the chorus starts.
DOUGLAS : Like what?
AMELIE : I don't know. Something a bit darker.
CHERLINE looks between them.

CHERLINE : Aren't we already in G minor?
AMELIE : Doesn't mean every chord has to sound the same.
She presses down a few keys, trying out a different progression. DOUGLAS leans over slightly to listen.

DOUGLAS : What about C minor?
AMELIE : Try it.
DOUGLAS joins her on guitar.

CHERLINE : Is that C minor I'm hearing?
DOUGLAS raises his thumb without looking up, his fingers still moving.

CHERLINE : Did you even hear me?
DOUGLAS : Yeah.
They play the progression again. ANDREA leans back slightly, listening. His eyes stay on the piano for a few seconds before he shakes his head.

ANDREA : Hmm... no.
AMELIE : No?
AMELIE looks over at him.

ANDREA : It's too dark.
DOUGLAS : Bit of a problem, considering you just said it was too bright.
ANDREA : I know. I'm saying that's too far the other way.
AMELIE : So somewhere in between.
ANDREA nods, thinking.

ANDREA : Yeah. Pretty much.
AMELIE changes one of the chords and plays the progression again. ANDREA suddenly lifts a hand.

ANDREA : Wait. That one.
AMELIE immediately stops.

AMELIE : This?
ANDREA : Yeah, keep that. I like that change.
AMELIE repeats the chord. ANDREA leans forward, listening more closely.

She moves into the next chord.

ANDREA : No, not that one. The next one.
DOUGLAS : Which next one?
ANDREA points towards the piano, trying to follow along.

ANDREA : The one after that.
DOUGLAS : That's incredibly helpful.
ANDREA : You know what I mean.
DOUGLAS : I probably do.
AMELIE plays through it again, this time following ANDREA's suggestion. ANDREA nods along, his fingers lightly tapping against his knee.

ANDREA : Yeah. That's it.
CHERLINE : Okay, that actually sounds nice.
CHERLINE leans forward a little, listening as they play the progression once more.

AMELIE : From the top?
ANDREA picks his guitar back up and settles it against his knee.

ANDREA : Yeah.
Everyone gets into position again.

ANDREA glances towards AMELIE before starting.

-- JUMP S2 : 5 MINUTES --

-- JUMP S2 : 5 MINUTES --

CHERLINE sits on the floor, eating her favourite pickle-topping pizza. Sauce is smeared around the corner of her mouth. AMELIE hands her a tissue.

CHERLINE : Oh, thanks, Em.
AMELIE : You're very welcome.

CHERLINE wipes her mouth and looks down at the tissue.

AMELIE : So, did you text him back?
CHERLINE : Who?
AMELIE : Blond-haired guy. From the Year Opening.
CHERLINE : Oh. Taylor?
AMELIE : That's his name?
CHERLINE : Sounds like it. I wasn't exactly taking notes.
AMELIE : He texted you, didn't he?
CHERLINE : Yeah. I'm not replying yet.
AMELIE : Why not?
CHERLINE : I don't know, girl.
AMELIE : You like him.
CHERLINE : Don't be so bold saying that.

AMELIE gives her a knowing look.

CHERLINE : Anyway, fancy a little drink after this?
AMELIE : Downtown?
CHERLINE : I thought Bronn's.
AMELIE : Downtown's fine.
CHERLINE : As long as we're not taking that horror alley.
JAKOVIC : I'm coming.

JAKOVIC drops into a crouch beside them.

CHERLINE : You weren't invited.
JAKOVIC : Didn't stop me hearing you.
AMELIE : You're actually coming?
JAKOVIC : Yeah. I don't wanna go home yet.
CHERLINE : Why?
JAKOVIC : Just don't.

CHERLINE looks at him for a moment.

AMELIE : I think WXRLD;END are playing at Downtown tonight.
CHERLINE : What?
AMELIE : Pretty sure I saw it on a flyer.
CHERLINE : And you're only mentioning that now?
AMELIE : You would've made it a whole thing.
CHERLINE : I wouldn't.
JAKOVIC : You are right now.
CHERLINE : Fuck off.

JAKOVIC steals a pickle from CHERLINE's pizza.

CHERLINE : Mate, what the hell are you doing?
JAKOVIC : You were distracted.
CHERLINE : Give me that.

She grabs it back.

JAKOVIC : So we're going Downtown, then?
AMELIE : Looks like it.
CHERLINE : Fine.
CHERLINE : But if they're not there, I'm blaming you.
AMELIE : Why me?
CHERLINE : You're the one who brought them up.
JAKOVIC : Fair.
CHERLINE : You're not helping.

-- JUMP S3 : NC --

DOUGLAS brings his leftover pizza to the bathroom. He's about to pee when his zipper gets stuck halfway. He needs both hands to free it, so he clamps the pizza between his lips.

ANDREA enters and sees DOUGLAS from behind. Neither of them seems particularly bothered by the lack of privacy.

ANDREA : Sorry about earlier. I know I was being a bit much. I just... I don't know. I hate when something feels off and we keep playing it anyway.
DOUGLAS finishes peeing and pulls his zip back up, the pizza still clamped between his lips.

ANDREA : And I wasn't trying to knock your arrangement or anything. I actually like what you guys had. I just couldn't get into it. Then we kept changing stuff and somehow everything sounded worse.
DOUGLAS takes the pizza out of his mouth.

ANDREA : And then we wait for William and he can't even come tonight. That's just brilliant.
A beat.

ANDREA : Anyway, Cher's been weirdly cheerful today. She was talking about some guy earlier too. Taylor, I think. You don't think that's why she's been less grumpy, do you? Or maybe it's Amelie. She likes this Taylor guy. I don't know. Don't you like her?
DOUGLAS gives him a quick glance.

ANDREA : Douglas, please. Say something.
DOUGLAS : What do you want me to say?
ANDREA : I don't know. An answer?
DOUGLAS : We're only friends.
ANDREA : You're so fucking useless.
DOUGLAS gives him the slightest grin.

DOUGLAS : Still here, though.
ANDREA : Yeah, unfortunately.
DOUGLAS : Shall we?
ANDREA sighs and follows him out of the bathroom.

-- JUMP S4 : 40M --

Night is still going, and the whole band except WILLIAM remains in the garage.

The three around the instruments are still at it. AMELIE sits at the piano, DOUGLAS beside her with his guitar, while ANDREA stands a few steps away, listening with his arms folded.

Across the room, CHERLINE sits at one end of the sofa, legs stretched out. JAKOVIC is lying across it with his head resting comfortably on her lap, one arm hanging off the edge.

CHERLINE : They're still on that?
JAKOVIC : Apparently.
CHERLINE : We've been here forever.
JAKOVIC : And we're still nowhere.
CHERLINE watches AMELIE play another variation.

CHERLINE : I kinda like this one.
JAKOVIC : You said that about the last one.
CHERLINE : The last one was shit.
JAKOVIC : So this one?
CHERLINE : Less shit.
JAKOVIC lets out a quiet laugh, then settles back against her.

At the piano, AMELIE stops playing.

DOUGLAS : It's terrible.
AMELIE : It's boring.
ANDREA : Yeah.
DOUGLAS : Great. So we're back to nothing.
AMELIE taps a few keys without looking at either of them.

AMELIE : What if we don't force the chorus to sound bigger?
ANDREA : Then what?
AMELIE : Make it smaller.
DOUGLAS : That's the opposite of what we were doing.
AMELIE : I know.
ANDREA thinks for a moment, then nods.

ANDREA : Worth trying.
JAKOVIC : Still considering letting me join you guys?
CHERLINE : Why are you being so stubborn?
JAKOVIC : Because I don't wanna go home.
CHERLINE : That's not my problem.
JAKOVIC : Come on. One drink.
CHERLINE : You said that already.
JAKOVIC : And I'm saying it again.
He sits up slightly.

JAKOVIC : I just need to get wasted tonight.
CHERLINE : Okay, okay. But just you. Don't invite the other boys. Deal?
JAKOVIC : Deal.
CHERLINE looks at AMELIE, then back at JAKOVIC.

CHERLINE : Jake, I've got an idea.

-- JUMP S5 : 30M --

Practice is over. Everyone is packing up. ANDREA, as usual, is responsible for the keys and locks the garage.

DOUGLAS is already putting on his helmet. AMELIE gets into CHERLINE's car.

DOUGLAS pauses.

DOUGLAS : Did you guys see Jake by any chance?
ANDREA : What?
DOUGLAS : Jake. Where is he?
AMELIE looks around.

CHERLINE : He's got something to do. Didn't you hear him earlier?
AMELIE : Did he say that?
DOUGLAS : I didn't hear anything.
ANDREA shakes his head, starts his motorcycle and gets on.

DOUGLAS : Well, let's call it a day, pal. See you.
ANDREA : Night, lad.
CHERLINE : Bye!
AMELIE : Bye!
ANDREA and DOUGLAS ride off.

CHERLINE takes out her phone and calls someone.

A few seconds later, JAKOVIC comes out from the side of the garage, phone in hand.

CHERLINE : They're gone.
AMELIE : You actually did it.
JAKOVIC : Obviously.
CHERLINE : Get in.
JAKOVIC gets into the car.

JAKOVIC : So where are we going?

-- JUMP S6 : 45M --

CHERLINE, AMELIE, and JAKOVIC arrive at Downtown. The bar is already fairly crowded. Music is playing through the speakers, and they can barely hear each other.

JAKOVIC : Why is it so crowded?
CHERLINE : Don't know.

JAKOVIC looks around the room.

JAKOVIC : Maybe because of that.

He points towards a poster in the corner of the room.

A WXRLD;END poster.

CHERLINE stops when she sees it.

CHERLINE : Oh, shit. They're actually here.

She looks at AMELIE.

CHERLINE : You knew?
AMELIE : I said I thought they might be.
CHERLINE : That's basically knowing.
AMELIE : I suspected.
CHERLINE : Barely.

At the counter, JAKOVIC catches their attention and makes their usual hand gesture for “the usual?” He follows it with a quick nod towards the drinks.

AMELIE and CHERLINE both nod.

JAKOVIC heads towards the counter.

CHERLINE : What are they doing here anyway?
AMELIE : Performing, presumably.

JAKOVIC returns with the drinks, a cigarette between his fingers.

JAKOVIC : Got a lighter?

AMELIE pulls out her lighter and hands it to him.

A familiar voice comes through the microphone.

People begin moving towards the stage. CHERLINE, AMELIE, and JAKOVIC follow, with JAKOVIC still struggling to light his cigarette.

TAYLOR, the vocalist of WXRLD;END, adjusts the microphone and looks out at the crowd.

Then he starts singing.

It's jazz.

Nobody seems to have expected it. WXRLD;END is known more for pop-rock, and even JAKOVIC looks up from his cigarette for a second.

CHERLINE is more interested than she means to be. She edges through the crowd until she can get a clearer view of the stage.

Halfway through the third song, their eyes meet.

CHERLINE drops her gaze.

Then she looks back.

TAYLOR is still looking at her.

The corner of his mouth lifts slightly before he turns his attention back to the performance.

The performance ends.

CHERLINE, AMELIE, and JAKOVIC sit near the counter, talking over the music.

From across the room, TAYLOR notices them and starts walking over.

Halfway there, two girls stop him to ask for a photo. He laughs, takes the pictures, then continues towards the table.

TAYLOR : Umm, hello?
The three turn around at the same time.

AMELIE : Hello!
CHERLINE : Hi.
TAYLOR : Did I disturb you guys?
AMELIE : Oh, no, no. We're just hanging around. Want to join us?
TAYLOR : Would be my pleasure.
TAYLOR sits in the empty seat beside CHERLINE.

CHERLINE looks straight ahead, suddenly very interested in the music coming from the speakers.

TAYLOR orders a drink.

AMELIE : Great performance, by the way.
TAYLOR : Thank you.
AMELIE : Is that your first time doing jazz?
TAYLOR : Oh, no. I used to sing jazz with my dad. Or my grandad, actually. They're both really into it.
AMELIE : Oh, nice.
TAYLOR looks at AMELIE.

TAYLOR : You're Amelie, right?
AMELIE : Yeah. These guys call me Amy.
He looks towards JAKOVIC.

TAYLOR : And you're... Jake?
JAKOVIC : Yeah. These guys call me Drumass.
He raises a hand in greeting.

TAYLOR : And... Cherline.
He looks towards her.

CHERLINE : Right.
TAYLOR : Oh, yeah. Sorry. Anyway, I'm Taylor.
AMELIE : We know.
CHERLINE : She's a big fan of WXRLD;END. She told me.
TAYLOR : Oh, really?
AMELIE : Yeah. I've already put at least two of your songs on my Spotify playlist.
TAYLOR : Oh... that's a decent number.
AMELIE : I'm messing around.
AMELIE suddenly gets to her feet.

AMELIE : Anyway, I should go to the toilet.
She grabs her bag, then looks at JAKOVIC.

AMELIE : Jake, come with me.
JAKOVIC : Excuse me? I'm not your servant.
AMELIE : Just take this.
She puts her bag in his hands and starts pulling him away.

JAKOVIC : The toilet's that way.
AMELIE : I know.
JAKOVIC : Then why are we going this way?
AMELIE : Just come on.
JAKOVIC looks back at CHERLINE and TAYLOR.

JAKOVIC : Oh.
AMELIE : Exactly.
JAKOVIC : Right.
They keep walking.

CHERLINE is left alone with TAYLOR.

TAYLOR : Hi.
CHERLINE : Hi.
TAYLOR : I saw you in the crowd earlier.
CHERLINE : I saw you on the stage.
They both laugh quietly.

TAYLOR : Anyway, we barely see your band performing lately. Everything alright?
CHERLINE : Yeah, it's fine. We're preparing for our own show, so that's kind of our priority at the moment.
TAYLOR : Oh, that's nice. Can I get an early ticket?
CHERLINE : It's a bit early for that. We haven't even thought about tickets yet.
TAYLOR smiles.

TAYLOR : Anyway... I texted you like a month ago. Did you change your number? It seemed like my messages weren't getting through?

END OF EPISODE 1
stories.synopsis: Mercy's practicing with their last song for the Summer Album. Cherline has a feeling to a boy she met earlier during Year Opening Concert, that also in a band called WXRLDSEND, Taylor Johannson. Amelie arranged something but things unexpected happen.

stories.title: Man with Prada
stories.body:
EPISODE 2

-- S1 : FLASHBACK --

Earlier that year, at a music festival on the outskirts of London, bands of all kinds are performing. Some are already well known. Others are still trying to make a name for themselves. MERCY is among them.

It is the first time CHERLINE and TAYLOR meet. Their sets happen close together. TAYLOR performs first, and the two briefly pass each other while CHERLINE is getting ready for MERCY's set.

Nothing happens.

MERCY performs. TAYLOR stays somewhere nearby.

At one point, his eyes catch the bracelet around CHERLINE's wrist. He looks at it for a little longer than he probably means to.

Later that same day, CHERLINE is with the rest of her band when TAYLOR approaches from behind.

TAYLOR : Hello.

He taps her shoulder.

CHERLINE : Hi!
TAYLOR : Oh, um... I'm Taylor.
CHERLINE : Cher.
TAYLOR : Nice to meet you.
CHERLINE : You too. You're...
TAYLOR : I liked your voice, by the way.
CHERLINE : Oh. Thanks.
TAYLOR : Is that bracelet handmade?
CHERLINE : Yeah. I made it myself.
TAYLOR : Thought so.
CHERLINE : Are you into crochet too?
TAYLOR : A bit, yeah.

He reaches for the small crochet guitar hanging from his bag.

TAYLOR : I've got one too.
CHERLINE : Oh, that's cute.
TAYLOR : And the little details on yours...
CHERLINE : Oh, you noticed.

She turns her wrist slightly.

CHERLINE : This random letter is actually the initial of one of my friend's names.
TAYLOR : Oh, nice.

He looks at the bracelet again.

TAYLOR : I've got a few more of these back home.
CHERLINE : Really?
TAYLOR : Yeah. I could send you some pictures sometime.
CHERLINE : I'd like that.

A small pause.

TAYLOR : Mind if I get your number?
CHERLINE : Yeah, sure.

CHERLINE opens her phone and starts giving him the number.

CHERLINE : It's... ███-███-07...2.

-- JUMP S2 : BACK TO PRESENT --

CHERLINE is still standing near the front of the bar.

CHERLINE : Shit.

-- JUMP S3 : GARAGE --

Outside the garage, WILLIAM stops in front of the half-open door.

WILLIAM : Oh, shit.
He looks at it properly.

The garage is almost never open this early. And, as far as he knows, none of them are supposed to be here.

WILLIAM walks towards the door.

-- JUMP S4 : STREET --

DOUGLAS is out for his morning run, earphones in.

His phone rings.

WILLIAM's name appears on the screen.

DOUGLAS answers.

DOUGLAS : I'll be there in a sec.
He hangs up, pulls the earphones from his ears and stuffs them into his pocket.

-- JUMP S5 : GARAGE --

DOUGLAS arrives at the garage.

He looks at the open door.

Then at WILLIAM's motorcycle.

Something about it catches his attention.

He walks closer and notices the key still sitting in the ignition.

He pulls it out, then heads inside.

From the doorway, he can already see WILLIAM at the little kitchen by the entrance, pouring himself a cup of tea.

DOUGLAS is still slightly out of breath from the run when he gets closer.

DOUGLAS : Someone trying to get in?
WILLIAM : Oh, Doug. Sorry.
WILLIAM gives him a small smile.

DOUGLAS : What?
WILLIAM : It's, uh... no one.
He points towards the sofa.

WILLIAM : But I found Andrea asleep there. Think he stayed here last night. I don't really know.
DOUGLAS : Oh.
WILLIAM : Yeah. I literally texted everyone, but no one answered. Except you.
He looks around the garage.

WILLIAM : Like, where the fuck have these people gone?
DOUGLAS : They're probably tired. We were practising until pretty late.
DOUGLAS looks towards ANDREA.

DOUGLAS : Anyway, you good?
WILLIAM : Yeah. Thanks for asking.
He takes a sip of tea.

WILLIAM : I'm more worried about him, honestly. Kind of weird finding him asleep here. Think he was playing around with the instruments too. Don't know.
DOUGLAS looks at ANDREA again.

They all left together last night. At least, that's how he remembers it.

DOUGLAS : You tried waking him?
WILLIAM : Yeah. He was on the floor earlier, so I moved him onto the sofa.
WILLIAM : Couldn't wake him up.
DOUGLAS : Mmhm.
WILLIAM : He must've just gone to sleep.
DOUGLAS : Right.
WILLIAM : Fancy a cup of tea?
DOUGLAS : Nah, I'm good. Just went for a run.
WILLIAM : Fair.
WILLIAM sits down with his tea.

WILLIAM : How was last night?
DOUGLAS : We were shit.
WILLIAM : That bad?
DOUGLAS : The arrangement was doing our heads in. Every time we changed something, we had to rework half the song. By the end, it didn't even sound like what we started with.
WILLIAM : Maybe that's why.
DOUGLAS : Could be.
WILLIAM's phone buzzes.

He looks down.

AMELIE.

WILLIAM : Amelie's finally answered.
He opens the chat.

MISSED CALL

MISSED CALL

WILLIAM : Answer.
AMELIE : Sorry, mate.
AMELIE : Just woke up, swear.
AMELIE : What's going on?
WILLIAM : Never mind.
AMELIE : Then why text me?
WILLIAM : I'll tell you later.
Something moves on the sofa.

WILLIAM looks up.

DOUGLAS does too.

ANDREA shifts slightly, but doesn't wake.

WILLIAM : You got anywhere to be?
DOUGLAS : Nah. Why?
WILLIAM : You just went jogging. Go home, have a shower or something. Come back later if you want.
He looks towards ANDREA.

WILLIAM : I'll wait for this kid to wake up. Probably slept pretty late.
DOUGLAS : Yeah. Fair enough.
WILLIAM : Take care.
DOUGLAS : You too.
DOUGLAS leaves.

-- JUMP S6 : 20 MINUTES EARLIER --

CHERLINE is still in bed.

The same pieces of last night keep coming back.

The wrong number.

TAYLOR.

The girl who kissed him.

She picks up her phone.

Turns it on.

Turns it off.

A few seconds later, she turns it on again.

Then off.

She eventually shuts it down completely and throws it to the other end of the bed.

CHERLINE gets up and walks around the room for a while.

She stops and reaches into her pocket.

She pulls out the little crochet record charm TAYLOR gave her.

She turns it over in her hand.

Looks at it for a moment.

Then attaches it to her bag.

-- JUMP S7 : BACK TO PRESENT --

DOUGLAS is on his way back home when his phone rings again.

WILLIAM : Where are you?
DOUGLAS : Like two turns away from my flat. Why?
WILLIAM : Cher's phone went dead when I called her. Can you go check on her?
DOUGLAS : Huh? What happened?
He sighs.

DOUGLAS : Alright. I'll go.
There is some noise in the background.

DOUGLAS : Has that kid woken up yet?
WILLIAM : Who?
He looks over.

WILLIAM : Oh. Yeah. He's awake. Eating instant ramen.
WILLIAM raises his voice.

WILLIAM : Woi, Andrea! Douglas is here!
ANDREA : Doug!
DOUGLAS : You alright there, buddy?
ANDREA : Yeah. I'm alive.
DOUGLAS : Right.
WILLIAM : Okay, Doug. Don't forget.
DOUGLAS : Yeah. I'll head back, grab the bike, then go get Cher.
WILLIAM : Okay.
The call ends.

WILLIAM watches ANDREA eat.

He is absolutely destroying the ramen.

ANDREA eventually notices.

ANDREA : What?
WILLIAM : Nothing.
ANDREA : Why are you looking at me like that?
WILLIAM points towards the far end of the kitchen.

WILLIAM : That ramen you're eating?
ANDREA looks over.

WILLIAM : It was in the cupboard over there. You could've just taken it.
ANDREA : Yeah, well... didn't know.
WILLIAM gives him a look.

WILLIAM : What were you doing here all night, anyway?
ANDREA stops.

He swallows what's left in his mouth.

He puts the noodle packet down beside him.

He doesn't answer straight away.

-- JUMP S8 : 30 MINUTES LATER --

A knock at the door.

DOUGLAS : Cher?
Inside, CHERLINE is looking through a drawer.

She stops and opens the door.

CHERLINE : Oh, hey, Doug.
DOUGLAS : Why weren't you picking up?
CHERLINE : Oh.
She looks at her phone.

The screen stays black.

Then she remembers.

CHERLINE : Oh yeah. I turned it off.
DOUGLAS : What for?
CHERLINE : Nothing. Phone was acting up.
She turns it back on.

CHERLINE : Think I need to buy a new one.
The screen lights up.

Notifications start coming in.

WILLIAM.

ANDREA.

DOUGLAS.

More from WILLIAM than anyone else.

CHERLINE : You guys called me like a ton. What happened?
DOUGLAS : William called me while I was jogging. He thought someone broke into the garage.
CHERLINE : What?
DOUGLAS : The door was open. He called everyone, but nobody picked up except me.
He shrugs.

DOUGLAS : Then I get there and Andrea's asleep inside.
CHERLINE : Andrea?
DOUGLAS : Yeah. Apparently he stayed there all night. Forgot to shut the door properly.
CHERLINE : Why was he even there?
DOUGLAS : Don't know.
A beat.

DOUGLAS : Got a few theories, though.
CHERLINE doesn't ask what they are. She goes back to looking through the drawer.

DOUGLAS : What are you looking for?
CHERLINE : My crochet needle. I lost one.
DOUGLAS : You're crocheting again?
CHERLINE : Don't know. Felt like it.
DOUGLAS : Mm.
CHERLINE : Can you take me to the crochet shop?
DOUGLAS : Yeah, sure.
CHERLINE : I need to restock anyway.

-- JUMP S9 : 20 MINUTES LATER --

DOUGLAS parks the motorcycle outside the shop.

They both take off their helmets.

DOUGLAS reaches out to help CHERLINE with hers.

CHERLINE : Thank you.
She looks towards the shop.

CHERLINE : Anyway, are you coming in too? Might take a while.
DOUGLAS : I've been distracted by that burrito place since we got here.
He points across the street.

DOUGLAS : I'll get one first. Then I'll come back.
DOUGLAS : You want one?
CHERLINE : Nah. Go on.
DOUGLAS : Okay then.
CHERLINE : Okay.
They split up.

CHERLINE goes into the crochet shop.

DOUGLAS walks towards a small burrito cart by the roadside.

DOUGLAS : One, please.
He waits.

He takes out his phone.

Before opening Instagram, he lowers the brightness.

A message from AMELIE is waiting.

AMELIE : There's always something going on this early.
DOUGLAS sends a laughing emoji.

AMELIE : You with Cher?
DOUGLAS : Yeah. Why?
AMELIE : Nothing. She disappeared last night.
DOUGLAS : What do you mean disappeared? Didn't she go home with you?
AMELIE : Yeah, she did. We went to the bar first. Tell her I'm fine. My messages weren't going through.
DOUGLAS : Ohh. So you were probably a bit drunk and slept in. Cher's phone was off.
AMELIE : Yeah, basically. Hehe.
DOUGLAS looks up for a second.

Then types.

DOUGLAS : Have you heard from Jake? He still hasn't read my messages.
A moment.

AMELIE : He came with us.
DOUGLAS stares at the message.

DOUGLAS : Good to know I wasn't invited.
AMELIE : Yeah.......... I should get ready. Boss Willie's calling me to the garage. Bye.
DOUGLAS : Bye.
He puts his phone back into his pocket.

The burrito is ready.

DOUGLAS pays for the burrito and heads back towards the shop. At almost the same time, CHERLINE comes out with several bags in her hands.

They sit on the bench outside.

DOUGLAS : That's quite a lot.
CHERLINE : A lot of the yarn ran out.
DOUGLAS : Amy said she's fine. She went home first last night.
CHERLINE : Fucking hell.

DOUGLAS takes a bite of his burrito.

DOUGLAS : How come Jake got invited and I didn't?
CHERLINE : It was supposed to be just me and Amy. He kept pushing to come. Said he wanted to get drunk.
DOUGLAS : Nice.
CHERLINE : It was supposed to be a girls' night. Somehow he turned it into something else.
DOUGLAS : Something else?
CHERLINE : There was...

She stops.

Something catches her attention across the street.

CHERLINE : Oh, shit.
DOUGLAS : What?
CHERLINE : Don't look.
DOUGLAS : Why?
CHERLINE : Just keep talking.
DOUGLAS : About what?
CHERLINE : Anything.
DOUGLAS : Alright. This burrito's actually shit.
CHERLINE : It's not.
DOUGLAS : It is.
CHERLINE : You just picked the wrong one.
DOUGLAS : There was a wrong one?

CHERLINE laughs despite herself.

She keeps glancing past him.

DOUGLAS : You're definitely looking at something.
CHERLINE : I'm not.
DOUGLAS : Right.

TAYLOR walks past behind them.

CHERLINE follows him with her eyes for a moment before looking away.

DOUGLAS notices and reaches over, giving her cheek a quick squeeze.

CHERLINE : Ow!
DOUGLAS : You're being weird.
CHERLINE : That hurt.
DOUGLAS : Good.

CHERLINE looks at him, then pinches his cheek.

DOUGLAS : Ow!
CHERLINE : Fair.

-- JUMP S10 : GARAGE --

Back at the garage, WILLIAM and ANDREA are still there.

AMELIE arrives a few minutes later.

Not long after, DOUGLAS and CHERLINE walk in.

ANDREA is still sitting on the sofa, looking half asleep.

CHERLINE : Wake up, sleepyhead.
She throws a ball of yarn at his head.

ANDREA : What in the fuck?
DOUGLAS : Morning.
CHERLINE : Where were you? I was looking for you last night.
AMELIE : I was looking for you too.
CHERLINE : Yeah? Where were you?
AMELIE : You mean with Jake?
CHERLINE : Speaking of Jake, where is he?
AMELIE : He's fine. He's not coming.
CHERLINE : Why?
AMELIE : He's got something to do.
WILLIAM taps his soda can against the table.

WILLIAM : Okay, lads.
Everyone looks over.

WILLIAM : Since I've already called half of you this morning, might as well get everyone together.
He puts the can down.

WILLIAM : There's something we need to talk about.
CHERLINE : What happened?
WILLIAM : The venue for our summer performance can't keep the date we agreed on.
DOUGLAS : Why?
WILLIAM : They've got some issue with the government or something. Whatever it is, they can't change it.
CHERLINE : So what now?
WILLIAM : Two options.
He counts them off on his fingers.

WILLIAM : We move the show two weeks to a month earlier.
WILLIAM : Or we move it to September.
CHERLINE : September? That's basically two months later.
WILLIAM : Exactly.
CHERLINE : So if we don't want to push it back that far—
WILLIAM : We perform earlier.
ANDREA stays quiet.

DOUGLAS : How much time would we have?
WILLIAM : Two or three months.
AMELIE : Not bad.
CHERLINE : Better than delaying it.
DOUGLAS : Yeah, but we'd have to plan those three months properly.
He looks around at everyone.

DOUGLAS : Like, properly. Otherwise we're not gonna make it.
CHERLINE : Agreed.
AMELIE looks at ANDREA.

AMELIE : What about you, Andrew ?
ANDREA looks around.

He thinks for a moment.

ANDREA : Yeah... okay.
A small pause.

ANDREA : Yeah, alright.
WILLIAM : So we're doing it?
ANDREA nods.

ANDREA : We're doing it.
stories.synopsis: William comeback to London at early morning, finding out the Garage was full of mess. Cherline had struggle with her feelings entire night.

stories.title: The Music Stop when The Lights On
Bring the Band on the Floor!
Stand by Me, Stand by You
They Told Me Im Wrong, So Be It!
Tell Me Its Not Over Yet
Where Do We Go From Here?
Such a Pity, Such a Pity
Epilogue
stories.body:
I used to think people stayed. Maybe because, for a while, we did.

We kept showing up in the same places, sitting beside the same people, making the same noise. It was easy to believe that was just how things were going to be.

Then Cher changed.

Then Jakov.

Not all at once. 
Not in some dramatic way. 
Just little things. 
A different plan.
 A different place.

Someone not showing up one night. 
Someone who used to be there suddenly having somewhere else to be.

And somehow, the world kept moving anyway.

I think I spent a long time trying to understand when things had started becoming different.

Maybe there wasn't a moment.

Maybe we just weren't paying attention.

Even now, Douglas is still Douglas. Amelie is still Amelie. Henry is still somewhere in the middle of whatever he's trying to figure out.

And the band...

Well.

It's not what it was.

I don't think it's supposed to be.

People carry things you don't see. 
They keep parts of themselves somewhere you can't reach.
Sometimes you find out.
 Sometimes you don't.

And maybe that's okay.

Maybe knowing someone isn't about knowing everything.

Maybe it's just being there long enough to see them become someone you didn't expect.

And still recognising them.

Still caring.

Even when you don't quite know where they're going next.

I don't know if we ever really stayed together.

Maybe we just kept finding our way back to each other.

And maybe that's enough.

Because in the end, that's what this was.

Not a place where everyone stayed.

Just a place where, for a while...

we found each other.

Glad that i found myself in these people i loved and i cared.
And tommorow, it's year 2021.
Au Revoir.

stories.title: Act I
stories.body:
What song had the moon written to bless the meadow where I sat that night? Fireflies wandered through the grass, insects played their tireless hymn, and the river held the moon in its dark, unsteady mirror. Balon had once tried to write all of it down. He had never found a sentence that pleased him.

In the middle of spring, in the year 615, Harricorian soldiers occupied the Hastelan plain. The cold war among three kingdoms had lasted two and a half years, long enough for the tents to look almost permanent. Their red canvas scattered across the pale-green fields like petals dropped by a careless hand. Rain the night before had left the roads shining with mud. By morning the camp had returned to its usual business: men shouting for breakfast, merchants haggling, horses protesting their harnesses, and someone singing badly in the distance.

Balon sat at a narrow desk in the herald's pavilion, finishing a letter that was not his to write. He read it once, checked the date, and rolled the parchment before tying it with a length of twine. It was the third letter he had prepared that morning. The first had been a formal notice, the second a request for provisions, and the third a greeting so polite that it had taken him longer than either of the others.

He inspected his hands. Ink stained the sides of his fingers and darkened the crease beneath one nail. The water bucket that normally stood near the pavilion entrance was missing.

Outside, the air had already grown warm. A boy selling roasted nuts hurried past him, followed by two soldiers arguing about a debt neither intended to repay. Beside the road, local families had set up makeshift stalls. They sold bread, wine, combs, buttons, mended clothes, and the promise of various entertainments. The camp was an army to its commanders. To everyone else, it had become a town that moved only when ordered.

Balon made his way between the tents and toward the trees. A stream joined the river beyond the busiest part of camp; he had washed there before. He took off his shoes, rolled up his sleeves, and crouched beside the water. The cold made him draw in a breath. He rubbed his fingers together until the ink began to loosen and drift downstream.

A movement overhead caught his attention. An owl sat among the branches, round-eyed and perfectly still.

"An owl?" Balon said. "At this hour?"

The bird offered no explanation. Balon watched it for another moment, then looked toward the sunlight slipping between the leaves. There was freedom in belonging nowhere in particular, he thought. Or perhaps that was a foolish thing to think about an owl, which probably had a nest and a very firm opinion about trespassers.

By the time he returned to the pavilion, his sleeves were damp and he had found the beginning of a sentence. He took a spare sheet from his bag and wrote, slowly, as if the words might startle and flee.

Then I went into the sun, breaking free, as an owl. But what was the cost of being free in a place I had never meant to be?

He read the line, pursed his lips, and crossed out the last half. He tried another ending. That was worse. After a minute he crumpled the whole sheet and threw it beneath his desk, where several of its predecessors had already gathered.

"If paper were expensive, you'd have bankrupted us by now."

Filipe stood at the entrance, carrying a cup of water and wearing the expression of someone who had been waiting to say that for some time.

"It is expensive," Balon replied.

"Then stop feeding it to the floor."

"It hasn't complained."

A clatter of hooves interrupted them. They stepped outside as a column of riders passed along the muddy road. Their cyan banners moved above the crowd, bright against the red Harricorian tents. A few soldiers watched in silence. Others kept talking, although more quietly than before.

"Hollanders," Filipe said. "What are they doing here?"

"Their king is on his way to Harricoral," Balon said. "He's come to see his sister."

"His sister?"

"Our queen."

Filipe watched the procession. "I thought we were enemies with the Hollanders."

"We were."

"And now?"

"Now their princess is our queen."

"That's all it takes?"

"Apparently."

Filipe frowned. "And what if the marriage falls apart?"

Balon thought of the letters waiting on his desk, each one declaring goodwill in increasingly elaborate language. "I suppose I'll have something interesting to write about."

He was turning away when he noticed a stranger near the roadside. The man had long blond hair, a maroon coat, and the pale complexion of someone who had not spent much time walking under a southern sun. He was listening to a conversation among several riders, but his attention seemed to drift beyond them, taking in the camp with open curiosity.

For an instant, their eyes met.

Balon looked away first. He had only been looking, yet he felt caught doing something he could not explain. He returned to his pavilion without looking back.

Time passed quickly the next day, as though the wind were pushing the sun across the sky. By evening, the soldiers were ready to celebrate the mere fact that evening had arrived. Music spilled from the larger tents, someone had hung lanterns over the square, and every brewer within walking distance seemed determined to empty his barrels before dawn.

Balon had finished his work late. He found a place on a bench near the musicians and decided that, for once, he would not spend the night worrying over sentences. One cup of beer became two. By the third, the music had improved considerably, although he suspected the musicians themselves had not.

He watched a woman dancing in the square, her skirt turning in a circle of lamplight. Around her, soldiers clapped out of rhythm. A pair of men attempted the same steps and nearly knocked over a table.

"Looking for company, sir?" A woman stood beside Balon's bench. He nearly spilled his beer.

"No, thank you. And I'm not a sir. Just a scribe, I'm afraid."

"We're having a little game in the corner," she said. "Good company, a little drinking. You might enjoy it."

Balon glanced toward the crowded table she indicated. "I'm already doing quite well at drinking badly by myself."

"I'm afraid he has promised me the rest of his evening."

A man had appeared at Balon's side. Blond hair fell to the collar of a maroon coat. Balon recognized him from the road before he recognized the hand extended toward him.

The woman considered them both, shrugged, and returned to the party. The stranger gave Balon a small, conspiratorial smile and offered a hand.

Balon took the offered hand before thinking to object. The stranger led him through the crowd, then released him in the cool air outside.

"What was that?"

"That woman looked suspicious."

The stranger paused. "You looked uncomfortable. I thought I could help."

"You could've asked."

"Would you have said yes?"

Balon considered this with more seriousness than the question deserved. "Probably not."

"I'm Jaime," he said. "I arrived with the Hollanders yesterday. And, mind you introduce yours?"

"Balon."

"You don't look very Hollanderian," Balon said, and immediately regretted it.

"My mother was Cesterian."

"It's all right. I hear it often," Jaime said.

Jaime glanced back toward the celebration. "You know this place better than I do. Would you show me around?"

Balon was about to say that there were several better times, beginning with tomorrow morning. Instead he found himself saying, "I suppose I could show you a few things."

They started at the bridge market, where lanterns hung beneath wooden awnings and smoke from the cooking fires rose into the air. Balon pointed out the Harricorian pies, a reliable cobbler, and a cider seller best avoided.

They passed the sleeping quarters, where a cluster of soldiers sang a song neither of them knew. The red tents stood close enough that Balon could recognize each by its patched canvas.

"Is that yours?" Jaime asked, pointing at a red tent.

"No. That one." Balon indicated a smaller tent a little farther down the road.

"Do you stay there alone?"

"With colleagues," Balon said. "When any of them remember to come home."

"I usually sleep near my work," Balon added. "The desk is sturdy."

Jaime stopped to look inside when Balon lifted the tent flap. There were folded blankets, boots that had not been cleaned, and a little stack of papers resting on a travel chest. Balon moved to block Jaime's view of the papers, then felt foolish for doing it.

"Do you write for yourself? May I read something?" Jaime asked.

"Sometimes. But you absolutely may not read it," Balon said, too quickly.

"I mean, not tonight. Most of it isn't finished."

"Then I'll ask again when it is."

He said it lightly, without pressing further. Balon found himself oddly grateful. They resumed walking before he could invent another excuse.

At the edge of camp the music softened behind them. Balon knew a path between the tents and the trees, narrow enough that the torchlight from the road could barely reach it. He hesitated at the entrance.

"There's somewhere I go when the camp gets too loud," he said. "But it's not much to see. And it's out of the way."

"I don't mind," Jaime said.

Balon studied him. People had asked about his writing before and lost interest as soon as he declined to read it. Jaime, for reasons Balon could not explain, still appeared interested in the person carrying the papers.

"All right," Balon said. "Fetch that torch."

Jaime carried the torch through the damp grass while Balon led him to a broad tree overlooking the river. The moon lay broken across the moving water. Jaime took in the view. "I can see why you come here."

They settled against the trunk. Jaime sat close enough to share the light but left a comfortable space between them. He drew his coat tighter around his shoulders. Balon spoke of the river in the morning, of the birds that gathered there, and of the sunlight that reached the grass before it reached the camp.

"Sorry," Balon said when he realized how long he had been speaking. "I've been talking too much."

"No, you haven't."

Jaime smiled but did not look away. Balon noticed that his attention had settled not on the river but on Balon's face.

"What?" Balon asked.

"Nothing," Jaime said.

"You've been staring," Balon said.

"Have I?" Jaime reached across the space between them and brushed a leaf from Balon's shoulder. He held it up between two fingers as though it answered everything.

"There."

"You could have told me," Balon muttered.

"I could have."

He dropped the leaf into the grass. Balon turned toward the water and discovered he could no longer remember what he had been saying about birds.

"What's in your pocket?" Jaime asked at last.

Balon looked down. The edge of a folded page showed beneath his coat. "Paper. Sometimes I think of a line while I'm walking and have to write it down."

"So you're a poet?"

"I'm a scribe. Being a poet would require producing poems worth reading."

Jaime glanced at the folded sheet. "Did someone teach you to write?"

"My uncle taught me to read and write. He works for the Duke of Erlons." Balon rubbed the crease in the paper with his thumb. "My father died when I was three. My mother is a carpenter. I grew up with my uncle for much of the time."

He had not planned to say so much. The information hung between them, suddenly more intimate than anything he had told Jaime about the river.

"Sorry," he added. "You didn't ask for all that."

"I did ask," Jaime said. "And it's impressive. Your uncle must be proud of you."

"What about you?" he asked. "Highborn?"

"I'm afraid so. Jaime Anders. My father is one of the Northlords. Our house is hardly the grandest, if that helps."

Balon rose abruptly, adopting a grave expression. "Step forward, son. One day all of this shall be yours."

Jaime got to his feet, playing along. "But Father, I'm not ready."

"Ready? A nobleman requires no such thing. Only a fine coat and somebody else to blame."

Jaime covered his mouth, already laughing. "You are a terrible father."

"A magnificent ruler, however. Historians will be very confused."

They laughed until Balon had to sit down again. The performance dissolved into imaginary ministers, debates over whether goats should hold public office, and the obligations of a royal baker. Jaime could match every foolish proposal Balon made, which only encouraged him.

When the laughter eased, Jaime sat beside him once again. Their shoulders touched for a moment as he settled against the trunk. Jaime made no comment and did not immediately move. Balon became very interested in straightening the folded edge of his paper.

"Do you bring everyone here?" Jaime asked.

"No."

"Why me, then?"

"I don't know," he said, which was as close to the truth as he could manage.

Jaime looked toward the river. "I'm glad you did."

For a while they listened to the river. The torch sank lower in its holder. Jaime talked about the road south and how strange the camp had seemed when he first arrived. He could speak easily about horses and weather, Balon noticed, but whenever a story became personal, he usually found something to laugh about instead.

At some point he told Jaime about the owl he had seen by the water. Jaime asked whether the bird had offered him any wisdom. Balon said it had looked disappointed in him. Jaime said that sounded like most of the scholars his father employed.

The moon moved above the branches. Balon remembered speaking, laughing, and being asked to move his shoulder because Jaime could not feel his arm. He remembered saying something about tomorrow, though not what. He remembered thinking that the silence between them had become comfortable.

He did not remember falling asleep.

Balon woke with his back against the tree and an entirely unreasonable dislike of daylight. His mouth was dry. The river, which had seemed so peaceful the night before, now made far too much noise. He sat up slowly and waited for the world to settle.

Jaime was gone, and the torch had burned out. Balon reached for the folded page he had carried the night before, but his pocket was empty. He searched the grass until the effort made his head ache.

He remembered the evening in pieces: the marketplace, Jaime laughing beneath the branches, and a leaf being lifted from his shoulder. He could not imagine why that last detail had survived when so many others had vanished.

"You look dreadful."

"It's nearly noon. Where were you? We were meant to meet last night," Filipe said.

"I'm sorry," Balon said. "I think I had a little too much to drink. And I would prefer not to discuss quantities."

Filipe put a hand on his shoulder just as Balon's stomach protested. He steered him away from the main road in time for Balon to empty what little remained of his dinner into the grass. Two passing soldiers changed direction with the practiced calm of men familiar with such mornings.

Filipe turned his face away. "I should have left you beneath the tree."

Once he could stand straight, Filipe helped him back to the pavilion. There was water, a spare blanket, and a stern instruction not to touch another beer for at least a week. Balon accepted the first two.

Balon slept until the light had shifted across the canvas. When he woke, the birthday greeting for Lord Solan's niece lay rolled and ready on his desk, waiting to be delivered to the manor in Fletchford.

"Morning," said a familiar voice from outside.

Jaime was sitting on an empty wine barrel beside the tent, looking absurdly awake.

"I heard Filipe give you advice about beer," Jaime said. "Very moving."

Balon rubbed his forehead. "Please tell me I didn't say anything ridiculous last night."

Jaime pretended to consider. "You appointed a goat to the royal treasury."

"That was a sound political decision," Balon replied.

Jaime laughed, then took a folded scrap of paper from his coat. Balon recognized his own handwriting, the ink smeared where the sheet had been folded carelessly.

"You dropped this when you fell asleep," Jaime said. "I didn't read it."

Balon took it, surprised. "Thank you."

"I thought a writer might miss his words."

"We have unfinished business," Jaime said.

"Do we?"

"You're my guide. I haven't seen the entire camp."

Balon glanced at the sealed scroll. "I can't today. I have to deliver this to Lord Solan's manor in Fletchford."

"Is it far?" Jaime asked.

"Not especially far," Balon said, with the confidence of someone who knew the path and owned no horse.

Jaime leaned forward. "May I come?"

Balon hesitated. Filipe had known him for years and seldom accompanied him on errands unless asked. Jaime, whom he had only just met, had already seen the one place Balon kept to himself.

"No," Balon said. Then, before Jaime's expression had time to change, "I mean—yes. If you want to."

Jaime smiled, not triumphantly but with such immediate pleasure that Balon looked away.

"I do."

Balon turned back into the pavilion and spent an unnecessary amount of time looking for the shoes directly beneath his chair.

They left the encampment by the southern road. Fletchford lay southwest of Harbor, near the Basilonian border. The country was quieter there than the disputed approaches to Mayar; whatever quarrels the kingdoms maintained, this stretch of road had not become one of them. Farmers still drove carts between the villages, and the distant fields were busy with the ordinary demands of spring.

Balon carried the scroll in a leather satchel. Jaime had brought no horse, having assumed, for reasons known only to himself, that the journey would be brief.

"How much farther?" he asked.

"Not far."

"You said that some time ago."

"It hasn't become any farther," Balon said.

They crossed uneven ground and climbed a narrow rise where the grass grew between stones. Jaime halted to catch his breath.

"Why are we taking this path? There's a perfectly good road over there."

"This is shorter."

"It is also attempting to kill me."

"It's a hill."

"A very ambitious hill," Jaime added.

"I should have brought my horse," Jaime said.

"And enjoyed the view while I walked behind you? How considerate."

"You could sit behind me."

"That would be rather strange," Balon said, raising an eyebrow.

"Because—" Balon stopped. He did not have a good answer that he wanted to say aloud. "Never mind. Shall we rest?"

They found a broad stone beside the path. Balon sat first and took up most of the flat surface. Jaime examined the remaining corner and nudged him until he moved over.

"You've taken the entire kingdom," Jaime complained.

"An exaggeration. I left you this corner," Balon said.

Jaime sat, their shoulders brushing. Balon shifted an inch, then stopped when he realized Jaime was making no effort to move away.

Balon opened his satchel and took out a round of hardbread, large enough to share. He broke off a piece. Jaime glanced at the bread, and then at the path.

"Are you hungry?" Balon asked.

"Not terribly."

His stomach answered on his behalf.

Balon handed him a piece. "Here."

Jaime accepted the bread with such speed that Balon laughed. He ate as though he had been denied food for days, scattering crumbs across his maroon coat.

"I thought nobles were taught to eat elegantly," Balon said.

"We are. This is an advanced technique for getting bread into my mouth," Jaime said.

For a few minutes they ate without speaking. Balon could see Jaime's pale hair shifting in the breeze. He focused on the path ahead, aware that their shoulders were nearly touching.

"Why were you at the encampment? I mean, beyond being Hollanderian."

"My party was stationed along the route. The king will pass that way on his return, and the riders are to keep it clear. I have nothing to do that requires me at this very moment."

Balon glanced at the fine fabric of Jaime's dusty coat. "So you decided to spend your free time ruining your shoes with a scribe?"

"I didn't know about the shoes."

"But the scribe?"

Jaime smiled a little. "I knew about him."

Balon looked down at his bread. He had asked a simple question and somehow arrived at an answer that could mean several things.

"You have unusually long eyebrows," Jaime said.

Balon blinked. "That's an unfortunate way to change the subject. Do they look strange?"

"No. I like them. They suit your face."

"Well. Thank you. You sound like my mother," Balon added, wincing at himself. "She used to say things like that when I complained about my face."

"Where is she now?"

"Harbor City."

Balon remembered wood shavings on his mother's workbench and her hands guiding timber into place. He had not visited for some time. He missed her more often than he admitted, though he rarely knew what to say when he sat down to write her a letter.

Jaime waited. For once, he made no joke and offered no easy change of subject.

Balon stood and brushed crumbs from his clothes. "We should keep moving. I promised to arrive before the afternoon gets away from us."

Jaime rose beside him. As they started downhill, he held out a hand to help Balon across a muddy patch. Balon could have crossed it perfectly well alone. He took the hand anyway, just long enough to find his footing on the other side.

"See that little spot down there?" Balon said, pointing beyond the trees where the roofs of Fletchford had begun to appear.

Jaime nodded. "Yes, I suppose."

"Come on. It's only a few more steps."

Unfortunately, the weather had other plans.

Within minutes, the sky darkened, and before either of them could think to find shelter, rain began pouring down upon the hills. What had seemed like a short walk to the manor turned into a hurried scramble through the increasingly muddy path.

"Well, that's just wonderful," Jaime muttered.

They quickened their pace, their shoes sinking into the wet earth with every step. By the time they reached the manor, both were thoroughly soaked.

Balon hurried up the stone steps and knocked on the wooden door.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

No answer.

He waited a moment before knocking again, this time harder.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

A muffled voice came from somewhere inside. Balon couldn't make out the words over the rain hammering against the roof.

"He's coming," he said.

Jaime glanced at him. Balon's jaw was trembling, though the man himself seemed too preoccupied to notice. One hand was tucked tightly beneath his coat, protecting the parchment scroll he had carried throughout their journey.

Jaime looked at the scroll, then at Balon's face.

At last, the door opened.

A middle-aged man stood before them, his silver beard neatly trimmed and a scattering of freckles visible across his pale cheeks.

It was Rascal Solan, an old friend of Balon's who had once lent him a helping hand during his time on the Hastelan Plain. Their friendship had endured ever since.

"Good heavens, look at you!" Solan exclaimed. "Come in. I thought the rain might keep you from arriving before dark."

He stepped aside, only to pause when he noticed the taller man standing behind Balon.

His eyes travelled from Jaime's mud-covered boots to his unfamiliar face.

Jaime noticed the inspection immediately.

"Oh, I'm Jaime," he said, offering a polite smile. "Balon's—"

"Guard," Balon interrupted.

Jaime turned towards him.

"Friend," he corrected.

Balon looked up at him.

Jaime looked back, perfectly composed.

Solan's eyes moved between the two men. Whatever explanation he had expected, it certainly hadn't been that.

"Well, come in, both of you. You're letting all the rain inside."

They entered.

Balon immediately reached beneath his coat and carefully retrieved the parchment scroll. He inspected its edges before handing it over.

"For the birthday," he said.

Solan took it, looking rather pleased.

"You managed to keep it dry?"

"Barely."

"Good lad. I was beginning to think I'd have to explain why my gift hadn't arrived."

Balon gave him a faint smile.

"Where's Ella?"

"In the kitchen, last I saw her. Go on, you'll find her there."

Balon nodded and disappeared through a doorway further into the house, leaving Jaime alone with their host.

For a moment, Jaime simply stood where he was.

He had expected the interior to resemble the exterior: old, weather-beaten, and rather neglected. From the road, the manor had appeared almost forgotten, with moss creeping over its stonework and ivy climbing the walls.

Inside, however, it was an entirely different place.

A magnificent stag's head hung above the fireplace, its antlers stretching wide across the wall. Beneath it, newly lit logs crackled softly in the hearth. A rich red carpet covered much of the floor, while tall candles stood in elaborate holders that appeared to be made of gold.

But it was the woodwork that held Jaime's attention.

Intricate carvings ran along the walls, framing the doorways and climbing the wooden pillars. Even the furniture had been decorated with delicate patterns, each piece seemingly chosen with particular care.

Jaime was familiar with such craftsmanship. He had seen plenty of fine furnishings in his father's household, and yet something about this room made him look twice.

Nothing seemed to have been placed there by accident.

He moved towards a cabinet, studying the small objects arranged upon its shelves.

Solan remained by the fireplace, quietly watching his guest's growing curiosity.

Jaime stopped before a teapot.

It was a curious little thing, its surface covered in intricate carvings unlike those he had seen elsewhere in the room. He leaned closer, examining the patterns along its lid.

"May I?" he asked, resting his fingers lightly upon it.

"Certainly."

Jaime lifted the teapot from its place and carefully removed the lid.

To his surprise, it contained dried tea leaves.

He brought it a little closer. A faint, earthy scent rose from within, slightly sharp but not entirely unpleasant.

He examined the leaves for another moment.

Solan watched him with quiet amusement.

"Not quite what you expected?"

Jaime glanced at him, then back at the teapot.

"Not particularly."

He replaced the lid with care, though his eyes lingered upon the carvings.

"Where did you get this?"

“Actually, it’s my friends. He died years ago.”

“Oh, my condolences.”

“Thank you. Anyway please suit yourself, im head to the kitchen, fancy something? A wine, or tea, or something i could get you?” Mr. Solan offer.

“Tea, would be fine.” Jaime answered.

“Certainly.” Mr. Solan head to kitchen.

In the other hand, Balon greet Ella yg lagi memasak sup. He knocked the wooden wall, and said “Happy Name Day.”

“Oh hey, thank you Baley.” Ella replied.

“Told you to stop call me that.”

“Why? I like it.”

“But I don’t.”

“Surely you do remember it’s my name day.”

“What make difference?”

“No, nothing. Anyway, with whom father talk with?”

“A friend of mine, he insist to come with me.”

“Filipe?”

“No, not him.”

Mr. Solan interupt their conversation. “He fancy a tea, and go grab any drink you wanted Baley.” Sembari dia menyicipi sup ella yg masih boiled diatas tungku api dan mengambil fancy wooden mug of him.

“Love you.” Mr. Solan kiss his daughter head and patting her head and go back to the main room.

Mr. Solan and Jaime voice started to mumbling again from the kitchen, the voice goes high and low, sometime it sounds far, sometime it sounds close, guess, they’re rapidly move from one to another. Balon and Ella only listened to what they talking, a faint smile come from their both.

Hours after, a dinner is ready to be served. Mr. Solan sat on a lord(?) seat, Ella later supposed to sit on his left side and Balon, is in the second seat on the right side, left the first one empty. Jamie was about to sit on it.

“Sorry, you can sit on my right side, it’s for someone.” Balon said

“Oh, sorry i don’t know.” Jaime apologize.

“It’s fine Bale. Please, sit here.” Mr. Solan mempersilahkan Jaime untuk duduk di sebelahnya.

“No Mr. Solan, if it’s belong to someone.”

“And do you reckon someone other than us here?”

“Uh, no I’m afraid. Ok, then.” Jaime menurutinya, ia pun duduk di kursi tersebut.

“If i may ask, who’s this seat belongs to?”

“Matthias, hopefully we’ll see him later today.” Mr. Solan answered.

“He’s coming?” Balon asked.

Mr.Solan nod his head.

Jaime face shows his cluelessness about who’s Matthias.

Ella come to the table with the main course, Jaime look at his hand movement when she’s arrange the table and pour the wine to every glasses there, and at last, traveled to her eyes. Ella catch his eyes.

“Hi.”

“Hi.” Jaime replied.

“Oh, I haven’t formally introduce myself to you.”

Jaime datang menghampiri Ella, ia berlutut dan tangannya mengambil lengan Ella, lalu menciumnya.

“I’m Jaime”

“Jaime what? seems you’re more like someone than a commoner.” Mr. Solan asked.

“Jaime Fletcher.”

“So, you’re from here.”

“No, my mother from Castire, and my father was Highlanders. But they’re travel around, do bussiness, and ended up on Mayar. I was born, and yeah, we know how Mayar ended up, so we moved to Hastelan, and there, I met Balon.”

“Its too much ain’t it?” Jaime melihat ke semua orang. Mereka semua menyimaknya.

“I didn’t even know those details.”

“Now you know.”

“Alright, tonight is not about me i reckon.”

Jaime left that morning
never to be seen or heard again.

That same summer, Sara gave birth to twins.
They named them Jaime and Jonas.

Baby Jaime died just days later.
they renamed Jonas… Jaime.

Thirty years later, Mathias Petyrson joined the resistance armies.
He fought in the Battle of Hastelan Redfield, the war that freed Haricor Borreau from Nassau.
He died on that battlefield.

Five years after, Ella passed away during a flu pandemic.

Joana and Jaime cared for Balon for the rest of his life.

He returned to that tree
years passed,
and more years still
until he finally took his last breath.

Balon died at the age of 68.

--=--

“For Jaime,
my dear friend,
and my dear love.”

--=--

I’m gonna love you for the rest of my life,

And to make things clearer, I want to say

I’m gonna love you for the rest of my life
